nameStory: The name 'sow-thistle' comes from the belief that pigs (sows) loved to eat this plant, though it's not actually a true thistle at all! The 'common' part of the name distinguishes it from its pricklier relatives. Despite the thistle name, this plant is much gentler to touch than real thistles.
description: Common sow-thistle is a tall, leafy annual plant that can grow 2-4 feet high with bright yellow dandelion-like flowers. It has deeply lobed leaves that clasp around the stem and produces fluffy white seed heads that blow in the wind. This European native has made itself at home throughout New England as a common weed in gardens, fields, and disturbed areas. When broken, the stems and leaves release a milky white sap.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves with smooth, soft edges (not spiny) that wrap around and clasp the stem with rounded 'ears' at the base. The leaves feel tender and slightly succulent when touched.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers that look like small dandelions, about 3/4 inch across, arranged in loose clusters at the top of the plant. Each flower head has many thin, narrow petals.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white dandelion-like seed heads that form after flowering, with seeds that have feathery parachutes for wind dispersal. The seeds blow away easily when disturbed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant growing 2-4 feet tall with a hollow, branching stem that contains milky white sap when broken. The sap has a slightly bitter smell.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, hollow stems that are often reddish at the base and release white, sticky sap when cut or broken. The sap may stain fingers temporarily white.

habitat: Common sow-thistle thrives in disturbed soils like gardens, farm fields, roadsides, and vacant lots throughout New England. It prefers rich, moist soils but tolerates poor conditions and is often found growing alongside other weeds like dandelions and plantains. You'll commonly spot it in areas where the soil has been turned over or disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic soft, lobed leaves forming a rosette close to the ground. Spring leaves are often more tender and less bitter than summer growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants shoot up tall stems and begin flowering from early to mid-summer, producing their bright yellow dandelion-like blooms. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and distinctive clasping leaves are visible.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering and producing fluffy seed heads well into fall. Seeds disperse on the wind, and plants begin to yellow and die back with the first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving no above-ground parts. Seeds overwinter in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Common sow-thistle produces a white, latex-like sap that was once used as a substitute for chewing gum by children in rural areas, and the young leaves are actually edible and nutritious when cooked, tasting somewhat like spinach!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with dandelions, but sow-thistle has tall stems with leaves that wrap around them, while dandelions have all their leaves in a ground-hugging rosette. Remember: if the leaves climb the stem, it's sow-thistle; if they're all at the bottom, it's dandelion.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, common sow-thistle isn't a true thistle at all - it's actually in the same family as dandelions and lettuce. True thistles have spiny, painful leaves, while sow-thistle leaves are soft and smooth to touch.
compareHints: Common sow-thistle has smooth leaf edges, while its cousin prickly sow-thistle has spiny, prickly leaves that hurt to touch. Perennial sow-thistle is much taller (up to 6 feet) and has creeping underground roots, while common sow-thistle is shorter and grows fresh from seed each year. The leaf-clasping habit with rounded 'ears' is consistent across all three species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Prickly sowthistle stands out from common sowthistle by its much sharper, more prominent leaf spines and the rounded ear-like lobes at the leaf base.
Perennial Sow Thistle is the tallest and most robust of the three sow thistles in New England.
